Synonymy is the notion of sameness of meaning. According to Saeed (2014),
synonyms are different phonological words which have the same or very similar
meanings e.g. couch/sofa, boy/lad, lawyer/attorney. Two words are synonymous: if
the substitution of one for the other does not change the truth value of a sentence.
Synonyms are almost never truly substitutable. These often have different
distributions along a number of parameters. They may belong to different dialects,
registers, styles of language, colloquial, formal, literary etc. or these may belong to
different situations, e.g. wife or spouse is more formal than old lady or missus.

Topic – 49 Logic and Truth Montague (1974) has hypothesized that the tools of logic
can help us to represent sentence meaning. The study of logic comes down from the
Classical Greek world, famously from Aristotle. The beginnings of logic lie in a
search for the principles of valid argument and inference. A part of this study is a
concern for the truth of statements and whether truth is preserved or lost by putting
sentences into different patterns. Truth here is taken to mean a correspondence with
facts, or the correct description of the states of affairs in the world. Mostly, the truth
is said to be empirical as we need some facts of the world to know whether a
statement is true or not. For instance, the truth of the sentence ‗My father was the
first man to visit Mars‘ depends on the facts about the life of speaker‘s father: If her
father did go to Mars and was the first man there then the sentence is true; otherwise,
it is false. Similarly, the empirical truth of ‗the earth revolves around the sun‘ depends
upon the facts of the universe.

                                SEMANTICS AND PRAGMATICS
                                        (ENG508)
Lesson 23 to 43
1.    The term Implicature accounts for what a speaker can imply, suggest or mean, as distinct from
      what the speaker literally says (Grice, 1975).
2.    Implicature - “any meaning conveyed indirectly or through hints, and understood implicitly
      without ever being explicitly sta ted” (Grundy, 2000).
3.    Implicature covers the family of verbs such as ‘imply, suggest, mean’, which refer to the meaning
      of an utterance as understood in a given context.
4.    British language philosopher, Paul Grice (1913- 1988), made remarkable contributions to the field
      of pragmatics
5.    Implicatures are context dependent.
6.    Conversational Implicature is implied by the speaker in making an utterance; it is part of the
      content of the utterance; it does not contribute to direct (or explicit) utterance content, and it is not
      encoded by the linguistic meaning of what has been uttered.
7.    Sara: will you eat some of this chocolate cake? Amna: I’m on a diet. is an example of
      Conversational implicature.
8.    GCI stands for generalized conversational implicature
9.    In generalized conversational implicature - “no special background knowledge of the context of
      utterance is required in order to make the necessary inferences” Yule, 1996
10.   GCI is a conversational implicature that is inferable without reference to a special context.
11.   John walked into a house yesterday and saw a tortoise is an example of GCI. (understood that this is
      not John’s house)
12.   A scalar implicature is a quantity implicature based on the use of an informationally weak term in
      an implicational scale.
13.   Scalar implicatures arise in examples e.g. ‘Some professors are famous’
14.   Classic examples of scales implicatures include numerals modals and adjectives
15.   PCI stands for Particularized conversational implicatures.

                                                                                                        3
                                                                               sajidsecluded@gmail.com

      Semantics and Pragmatics (ENG508)                                                   Lesson 23~43

16.   Particularized conversational implicatures (PCIs) are the inferences which are worked out while
      drawing totally on the specific context of the utterance.
17.   In PCIs most of the time, our conversations take place in a very specific context in which locally
      recognized inferences are assumed (Yule, 2002).
18.   Cancellability is one of the properties of conversational implicature. It is also known
      as defeasibility.
19.   A conversational implicature is attached to the semantic content of what is said, not to the linguistic
      form i.e. it is possible to use a synonym and keep the implicature intact.
20.   Speakers try to convey conversational implicatures and hearers are able to understand them suggests
      that implicatures are calculable.
21.   Conventional implicature is not based on the cooperative principle or the maxims.
22.   Conventional implicature do not have to occur in a conversation (but in context). They do not
      depend on special contexts for their interpretation.
23.   Conventional implicature are associated with specific words that result in additional conveyed
      meanings when used. The English conjunction ‘but’ is one of these words.
24.   English words such as ‘even’ and ‘yet’ also have conventional implicatures.
25.   Conventional implicature do not make any contribution to truth conditions.
26.   Conventional implicature is associated with speaker or utterance rather than a sentence.
27.   Conventional implicatures are an arbitrary part of the meaning, and must be learned ‘ad hoc’.
28.   Conventional implicatures are not calculable via any natural procedure but are rather given by
      convention, thus they must be stipulated.
29.   Strong implicature is a communicated implication of an utterance which is the main communicative
      point of the utterance.
30.   Strong implicature is implicature that is related directly by the spoken utterances
31.   Strong implicature is that premises and conclusions which the hearer is strongly encouraged but not
      actually forced to supply.
32.   Weak Implicature is a communicated implication of an utterance which is not by itself the main
      communicative point of the utterance.
33.   Weak implicature is the weaker the encouragement, and the wider the range of possibilities among
      which the hearer can choose, the weaker the implicatures. For example, John: What are you
      planning to do today? Mary: I’m tired.

                                                                                                      4
                                                                              sajidsecluded@gmail.com

      Semantics and Pragmatics (ENG508)                                                     Lesson 23~43

34.   Any linguistic form that we use to accomplish the task of ‘pointing out’ is called deixis expressions.
35.   When you notice a strange object and ask, ‘What is that?’, you are using a deictic expression (that)
      to indicate something in the immediate context.
36.   Deixis is also called indexical expressions.
37.   The function of indexical expressions is to tell us where to look for a reference.
38.   Reference is mostly related to a particular person, place or time.
39.   Deixis is also known as the ‘Indexicality of language’ as it operates as indexes of specific meaning
      in a context.
40.   Spatial deixis include (here, there, this, that)
41.   Temporal deixis include (now, then)
42.   Person deixis include (you, me, she, him)

15.   PCI stands for Particularized conversational implicatures.

                                                                                                        3
                                                                               sajidsecluded@gmail.com

      Semantics and Pragmatics (ENG508)                                                   Lesson 23~43

16.   Particularized conversational implicatures (PCIs) are the inferences which are worked out while
      drawing totally on the specific context of the utterance.
17.   In PCIs most of the time, our conversations take place in a very specific context in which locally
      recognized inferences are assumed (Yule, 2002).
18.   Cancellability is one of the properties of conversational implicature. It is also known
      as defeasibility.
19.   A conversational implicature is attached to the semantic content of what is said, not to the linguistic
      form i.e. it is possible to use a synonym and keep the implicature intact.
20.   Speakers try to convey conversational implicatures and hearers are able to understand them suggests
      that implicatures are calculable.
21.   Conventional implicature is not based on the cooperative principle or the maxims.
22.   Conventional implicature do not have to occur in a conversation (but in context). They do not
      depend on special contexts for their interpretation.
23.   Conventional implicature are associated with specific words that result in additional conveyed
      meanings when used. The English conjunction ‘but’ is one of these words.
24.   English words such as ‘even’ and ‘yet’ also have conventional implicatures.
25.   Conventional implicature do not make any contribution to truth conditions.
26.   Conventional implicature is associated with speaker or utterance rather than a sentence.
27.   Conventional implicatures are an arbitrary part of the meaning, and must be learned ‘ad hoc’.
28.   Conventional implicatures are not calculable via any natural procedure but are rather given by
      convention, thus they must be stipulated.
29.   Strong implicature is a communicated implication of an utterance which is the main communicative
      point of the utterance.
30.   Strong implicature is implicature that is related directly by the spoken utterances
31.   Strong implicature is that premises and conclusions which the hearer is strongly encouraged but not
      actually forced to supply.
32.   Weak Implicature is a communicated implication of an utterance which is not by itself the main
      communicative point of the utterance.
33.   Weak implicature is the weaker the encouragement, and the wider the range of possibilities among
      which the hearer can choose, the weaker the implicatures. For example, John: What are you
      planning to do today? Mary: I’m tired.

                                                                                                      4
                                                                              sajidsecluded@gmail.com

      Semantics and Pragmatics (ENG508)                                                     Lesson 23~43

34.   Any linguistic form that we use to accomplish the task of ‘pointing out’ is called deixis expressions.
35.   When you notice a strange object and ask, ‘What is that?’, you are using a deictic expression (that)
      to indicate something in the immediate context.
36.   Deixis is also called indexical expressions.
37.   The function of indexical expressions is to tell us where to look for a reference.
38.   Reference is mostly related to a particular person, place or time.
39.   Deixis is also known as the ‘Indexicality of language’ as it operates as indexes of specific meaning
      in a context.
40.   Spatial deixis include (here, there, this, that)
41.   Temporal deixis include (now, then)
42.   Person deixis include (you, me, she, him)

Syllabus: Lesson 23-43 (Topics 114-225)
 Q. Driving force behind the Grice, s work (Topic#114)
 The fact that “what we literally say and what we clearly mean often differ is intuitively obvious but difficult
 to describe or explain systematically, was the driving force behind Grice's work. He was Interested in
 developing a systematic explanation of how and why literal and intended meaning differs. Implicatures are
 context-dependent.

Q. What is implicature? (Topic#114)
The term “Implicature” accounts for what a speaker can imply, suggest or mean, as distinct from what the
speaker literally says (Grice, 1975). Any meaning conveyed indirectly or through hints, and understood
implicitly without ever being explicitly stated.
Example:
Sara: My brother has just told me that he cannot look after our daughter after all.
Irum: He’s such a considerate man!
Explanation:
Here, we have clear sense that literal meaning of irum ‘s word cannot tell us everything what she meant,
without particular knowledge of the talk. It perhaps most likely that she is speaking sarcastically or she might
genuinely believe that he is a considerate man.

Q: What is the difference between generalized and particular conversational
implicature? (Topic#116)
Generalized Particular: It is a conversational implicature that is inferable without reference to a special context
(no special knowledge is required to figure out the additional meaning). It means that a generalized
conversational implicature is one which does not depend on particular features of the context, but is instead
typically associated with the proposition expressed.
A particularized conversational implicature occurs when a conversation takes place in a very specific context in
which locally recognized inferences are assumed.
EXAMPLE:
1) “Fred thinks there is a meeting tonight”.
Fred doesn’t know for sure that there is a meeting tonight.
2) A: Did you invited bella and Cathy?
B: I invited Bella.

Your young sister is drawing something. The action “draw “of young sister would ordinarily not convey
anything about her book, so implicature in this case depends on the context as well as the utterance itself.
2.A: hey, coming to the party tonight?
B: My parents are visiting.
Occur when a conversation takes place in a very specific context in which locally recognized inferences are
assumed. The particularized conversational implicature is used widely, because it can provide with
more contents, more aspects of speech than generalized conversational implicature.

Q: What is scalar implicature? (Topic#117)
A scalar implicature is a quantity implicature based on the use of an informationally weak term
in an implicational scale. Example Some professors are famous, where the speaker ‘s use of some typically
indicates that s/he had reasons not to use a more informative term .e.g. all. Some professors are famous,
therefore, give rise to the implicature that not all professors are famous. Similarly, in the utterance, some of the
boys went to the party, the word some implicates "not all of the boys went to the party. "Classic examples of scales
include numerals (< … three, two, one>), modals (<necessarily, possibly>, <must, should, may>), connectives
(<and, or>), adverbs (<always, often, sometimes>), degree adjectives (<hot, warm>) and verbs of ranking
(<know, believe>, <love, like>) or completion (<start, finish >).

Q: Write the Properties of conversational implicature. (Topic#119)
Non-detachability - a conversational implicature is attached to the semantic content of what is said, not to the
linguistic form i.e. it is possible to use a synonym and keep the implicature intact. It will not be detached from
the utterance as a whole, even though the specific words may be changed.
Reinforceability - Implicatures can be reinforced, e.g. John answered most of the questions. But he wasn't
able to answer the last question. (not redundant)
Non-conventionality - implicature is not carried by what is said, but only by the saying of what is said, or by
putting it that way. '
Calculability — speakers try to convey conversational implicatures and hearers are able to understand them
suggests that implicatures are calculable.

Q. Define cancellability. (Topic#119)
Cancellability is one of the properties of conversational implicature. It is also known as defeasibility. Presence
of a conversational implicature relies on a number of factors such as the conventional meaning of words used,
the linguistic and situational contexts, etc. So if any of them changes, the implicature will also change.
Example
1) John has 3 cows.
2) John has only three cows.

Enlist the procedure involved in the empirical research design.

Very often empirical research of this sort tries to determine whether there is a significant, as
opposed to a chance, association between two variables. For example: whether there is a
significant association between age and understanding of indirect speech acts as demonstrated by
the compliance with indirect requests.

Strong Implicature?

Strong implicature is a communicated implication of an utterance which is the main
communicative point of the utterance. The idea is that sometimes a speaker intends that her
hearer grasp a particular implication without which the utterance would not be relevant. Strong
implicature is implicature that is related directly by the spoken utterances or is that premises and
conclusions which the hearer is strongly encouraged but not actually forced to supply.

Quality and relation maxim?

Grice identified the Cooperative Principle as a ‗super principle ‘or a ‗supreme principle ‘(1989)
that he generalized from four conversational ‗maxims ‘. He identifies these maxims as follow:

Maxim of quantity – says that speaker should be as informative as is required. They should give
neither too little information nor too much.

Maxim of Quality – information provided in conversation to be genuine and justified.

Maxim of relation – says that speakers are assumed to be saying something that is relevant to
what has been said before.

Maxim of manner – says that we should be brief and orderly, and avoid obscurity and
ambiguity.

Grice said that hearers assume that speakers observe the cooperative principle and that it is the
knowledge of the maxims that allows hearers to draw inferences about the speakers ‘intentions
and applied meaning.

Metaphor and Synecdoche?

Metaphor is a type of figurative speech. Typically, a metaphor ascribes to an entity a property
that it does not, strictly and literally speaking, possess, although not all metaphors fit this
definition. Metaphors are not restricted to any particular type of word or phrase (Allott, 1988).
The metaphorical element of a sentence can be a noun phrase, as in ‗John is an iceberg. ‘Verbs
can also be used metaphorically, as in ‗Flintoff drilled the ball to the boundary. ‘

Synecdoche is a figure of speech in which an expression that denotes the part of something is
used to refer to the whole. For example, ‗mouth ‘in ‗I‘ve got six hungry mouths to feed‘. For
example: ‗willow ‘for cricket bat in such phrases as ‗to wield the willow ‘(Allott, 1988).

Here are two examples of making a promise:

   1) "I'll meet you at the library at 3 pm tomorrow."
   2) "Don't worry, I'll finish the project by the end of the week."

These statements commit the speaker to a specific action or outcome, making them promises.

Co-textual Context?

The context of the text itself is known as co-text. For example, ‗She is talking to her boss. ‘We
see, in this example ‗her ‘is pointing back to ‗She ‘. The words used in the conversation give
enough knowledge about ‗what has been mentioned before? and what is going to be ‘? The co-

text of a word is the set of other words used in the same phrase or sentence. Co-text limits the
range of possible interpretations we might have for a word. Consider a complicated example to
understand co-textual context. ‗She met (her) school teacher.

‘We get two situations here: First, ‗She ‘may have been used for a mother who met school
teacher of ‗her ‘(her daughter). Secondly, ‗She ‘may have been used for a lady who met her own
teacher. ‗I met a boy who was very brilliant. ‘In this example, ‗who ‘is pointing back to ‗the
boy whom I met ‘. With the analysis of previous examples, we can say, Co-Textual Context
cannot be ignored in pragmatics to interpret the meaning of the text. Co-textual context can be in
a sentence or within sentences.

Maxim violation?

Maxim violation is unostentatiously, quiet deceiving. Violating the maxim Quantity – Husband:
How much did that new dress cost? Wife: Less than the last one. Here, the wife covers up the
price of the dress by not saying how much; thus, not giving the required information to the
husband and violating maxim of quantity.

Violating the maxim Quality – Considering the same example, the wife when asked ‗How
much did that new dress cost? ‘It could have violated the maxim of quality by not being sincere
and giving him the wrong information i.e. thirty-five hundred rupees.

Violating the maxim relation – Similarly, in answer to ‗How much did that new dress cost? the
wife tries to distract him and change the topic saying: I know, let ‘s go out tonight. Now, where
would you like to go? This shows the violation of the maxim of relation.

Violating the maxim manner – In answer to ‗How much did that new dress cost? ‘, if she said
that ‗a tiny fraction of my salary, though probably a bigger fraction of the salary of the women
that sold it to me ‘, Hoping that it could be taken as an answer and the matter could be dropped.
It is, thus, like the wife answers the question in a way that could be said to be violating the
maxim of manner, in that she says everything except what the husband wants to know.

Deictic Center?

Deictic Center is when we hear a deictic, we typically make a number of assumptions about the
context. For instance, when we hear an utterance like ‗The postbox is on the left ‘we have to
decide whether the postbox is on the left in relation to the speaker or the hearer. The default
deictic center is the speaker ‘s location at the time of utterance.

Intertextual?

Intertextual refers to the relationship between two or more texts that are connected through
shared meanings, themes, or language. This connection can be explicit or implicit, and it can
involve:

   1) Quotations or references to other texts.
   2) Allusions to myths, legends, or historical events.
   3) Shared themes, motifs, or symbolism.

Q. conditions for promise 3
When the speaker promises to do something, there are two preparatory conditions: First, the event
will not happen by itself. Second, the event will have a beneficial effect.
Q. Conditions for warning
When the speaker utters a warning, there are the following preparatory conditions: It is not clear
that the hearer knows the event will occur. The speaker does think the event will occur. The event
will not have a beneficial effect.
Q. describes Macro function of languages?
Brown and Yule (1983) describe the ‗transactional‘ functions and the ‗interactional‘ function of
language. The „transactional‟ is the function which language serves in the expression of content
and the transmission of factual information. The „interactional‟ is the function involved in
expressing social relations and personal attitudes, showing solidarity and maintaining social
cohesion. At the extreme end of the interactional is „phatic communion‟ - language with no
information content used purely to keep channels of communication open. Brown and Yule
pointed out that much of the everyday human interaction is characterized by the primary
interpersonal rather than the primarily transactional use of language.

pre-sequences, insertion sequences, and opening and closing sequences.

Solidarity strategy is the tendency to use positive politeness, emphasizing closeness between the
speaker and the hearer. It will include personal information, use of nicknames, sometimes even
abusive terms (particularly among males), and shared dialect or slang expressions. A solidarity
strategy will be marked via inclusive terms such as ‗we‘ and ‗let‘s‘, for example in the party
invitation as in: ‗Come on, let‘s go to the party. Everyone will be there. We‘ll have fun‘.

Q. cognitive pragmatics 3
According to Bruno G.Bara (2010), Cognitive pragmatics focuses on the mental states and, to
some extent, the mental correlates of the participants of a conversation. The mental processes of
human communication are based on three fundamental concepts: cooperation, sharedness, and
communicative intention. These three fundamentals were proposed by Grice in 1975, though each
has since been refined by other scholars. The cooperative nature of communication is justified by
the evolutionary perspective through which the cooperative reasoning underlying a conversation
is explained. Sharedness accounts for the possibility of comprehending non-standard
communication such as deceit, irony, and figurative language (Bruno G.Bara, 2010).

According to Ide and Inoue (1991), Japanese women of higher social status tend to use more elaborated honorifics to
signal beauty, grace, and dignity. Ide(2005) uses the term ―beautification‖ honorifics, a form of gendered language

It has been observed in India and Pakistan that English is used as a dominant language in the elite class which shows
that this class is influenced by western culture. Errington states that language is sometimes ―gender-neutral‖ in
Asian Culture. Examples of the gender-neutral features are: The lack of gender marking with articles, or morphemes
on nouns; specific lexemes like ―human‖ or ―person‖ are not marked for feminine or masculine. The local greeting
is how many ―older and younger siblings do you have‖ rather than how many ―brothers and sisters do you have‖
(Atkinson and Errington 1990).

When the speaker utters a warning, there are the following preparatory conditions: It is not clear that the hearer
knows the event will occur. The speaker does think the event will occur. The event will not have a beneficial effect.

Brown and Yule (1983) describe the ‗transactional‘ functions and the ‗interactional‘ function of language.

The „transactional‟ is the function which language serves in the expression of content and the transmission of
factual information. The „interactional‟ is the function involved in expressing social relations and personal attitudes,
showing solidarity and maintaining social cohesion.

At the extreme end of the interactional is „phatic communion‟ - language with no information content used purely
to keep channels of communication open. Brown and Yule pointed out that much of the everyday human interaction
is characterized by the primary interpersonal rather than the primarily transactional use of language.

Solidarity strategy is the tendency to use positive politeness, emphasizing closeness between the speaker and the

‗we‘ and ‗let‘s‘, for example in the party invitation as in: ‗Come on, let‘s go to the party. Everyone will be there.

According to Bruno G.Bara (2010), Cognitive pragmatics focuses on the mental states and, to some extent, the
mental correlates of the participants of a conversation. The mental processes of human communication are based on
three fundamental concepts: cooperation, sharedness, and communicative intention. These three fundamentals were
proposed by Grice in 1975, though each has since been refined by other scholars.

The cooperative nature of communication is justified by the evolutionary perspective through which the cooperative
reasoning underlying a conversation is explained. Sharedness accounts for the possibility of comprehending non-
standard communication such as deceit, irony, and figurative language (Bruno G.Bara, 2010).

ENG508_Glossary

1. Anthropologist :An anthropologist is a person engaged in the practice of
   anthropology. Anthropology is the study of various aspects of humans within past
   and present societies. Social anthropology, cultural anthropology, and
   philosophical anthropology study the norms and values of societies.
2. Aspect :Tense is a category which allows a speaker to relate situations to time
   whereas aspect system allows speaker to relate situation and time and to view an
   event in various ways such as complete or incomplete.
3. Collocation :Collocation is a familiar grouping of words.
4. Compositional Semantics :Compositional semantics deals with the way that the
   meanings of lexical items combine to give phrase and sentence meaning.
5. Davidsonian Semantics :Davidsonian semantics argues that we can do
   semantics without possible worlds. Davidsonian Semanticists agree with other
   formal semanticists that the meaning of a sentence consists in its truth-conditions,
   but think that possible worlds and the like are not the right way to think about
   truth conditions.
6. Deontic Modality :Deontic Modality is where the verbs mark the speaker’s
   attitude to social factors of obligation, responsibility and permission.
7. Epistemic Modality :Epistemic Modality expresses the degree of knowledge
   that how sure is the speaker in his communication.
8. Evidentiality :Evidentiality is a semantic category which allows a speaker to
   communicate his/her attitude to the source of his/her information.
9. Formal Grammar :The study or the use of rules about how words change their
   form, and combine with other words to express meaning.
10. Hyponym :A hyponym includes the meaning of a more general word.For
   example, sister and mother are hyponyms of ‘woman’.

By ASFAND YARR

                              ENG508_Glossary

11. Idioms :Idioms are expressions "whose meaning cannot be inferred from the
   meaning of its parts”.
12. Moneo :‘Money’ is related to Latin ‘moneo’ (warn) because money was made
   in the temple of the goddess Juno Moneta.
13. Non-literal meaning :Non-Literal Meaning are instances where the speaker
   deliberately describes something in untrue or impossible terms in order to achieve
   special effects.
14. Paradigm :A paradigm is a set of linguistic or other units that can be
   substituted for each other in the same position within a sequence or structure.
15. Phrasal verb :A very common type of idiom in English is ‘phrasal verb’ the
   combination of verb plus adverb of the kind.
16. Pragmatics :Pragmatics concerned with the transmission of meaning through
   language in use.
17. Presupposition :Presupposition refers to the assumptions implicitly made by
   the speakers and the listeners.
18. Principle of compositionality :This says that the meaning of a piece of
   language is based solely on the meaning of its parts, and the way they are put
   together. Here the infinity and creativity of language are comprehensible.
19. Signification :This process of creating and interpreting symbols is called
   signification - far wider than language.
20. Signified :The concept that a signifier refers to is called signified.
21. Syntagmatic relations :Syntagmatic relations hold between two or more
   words co present in a sequence.
22. Thematic roles :Thematic roles mean the roles that referents of the arguments
   of a verb play in the event or as the state that the verb denotes.

By ASFAND YARR

                              ENG508_Glossary

23. Traditional logic :Logicians tend not to talk about ‘ideas’ though; the basic
   unit of traditional logic is the ‘proposition’; a significant term in the discussions
   of meanings.
24. Utterance :An utterance is an instance of the production of a sentence or a
   fragment of a sentence.

                                              Lesson 10
     Montague (1974) has hypothesized that the tools of logic can help us to represent sentence
      meaning. The study of logic comes down from the Classical Greek world, famously from Aristotle.

     The beginnings of logic lie in a search for the principles of valid argument and inference.

     A part of this study is a concern for the truth of statements and whether truth is preserved or
      lost by putting sentences into different patterns.

     Truth here is taken to mean a correspondence with facts, or the correct description of the
      states of affairs in the world.

     Mostly, the truth is said to be empirical as we need some facts of the world to know whether a
      statement is true or not.

     For instance, the truth of the sentence ‗My father was the first man to visit Mars‘ depends on
      the facts about the life of speaker‘s father:

     If her father did go to Mars and was the first man there then the sentence is true; otherwise, it
      is false. Similarly, the empirical truth of ‗the earth revolves around the sun‘ depends upon the
      facts of the universe..

     The term propositional logic‘ is also known as ‗propositional calculus‘ and ‗sentential
      calculus‘.

     Here, we are concerned with the relations that hold between sentences, involving complex
      sentences, irrespective of the internal structure of the sentences themselves.

     For example, we have two sentences i.e. ‗John is in his office‘ and ‗John is at home‘. Between
      them, one is true; if the second is false, it can be concluded that the first is true.

     This conclusion can be drawn irrespective of the form of the sentences themselves.
     Semanticists call a sentence‘s being true or false based on its truth value, and call the facts that
      would have to obtain in reality to make a sentence true or false, its truth conditions.

                                                  Lesson-9

                             Lexical Semantics: Fields and Collocations

    Many of the basic ideas in this topic are derived from de Saussure‘s notion of ‗value‘.
    He pointed out that a knight on a chess board is a knight not because of any inherent quality (shape, size,
     etc.), but because of what it can do in relation to the other pieces on the board (Saussure, 1959:110).
    He stressed this relational aspect of language, saying that there were ‗only differences and no positive
     terms‘.
    As differences are in some way related. For instance, he argued that ‗sheep‘ in English has a different
     value from ‗mouton‘ in French because English has also the word ‗mutton‘.
    Meanings of words have their association with other words which can be in the form of paradigmatic/
     syntagmatic relations, sense relations, collocation and idiomatic relations.
    Paradigmatic relations hold between concepts belonging to the same grammatical category.
    These relations cover a wide variety of associations between words, including morphological and phonetic.
    For instance, in a ‗red door‘ and ‗green door‘, ‗red‘ and ‗green‘ are in a paradigmatic relation to each
     other.
    A paradigm is a set of linguistic or other units that can be substituted for each other in the same position
     within a sequence or structure.
    In this sense, it may be constituted by all words sharing the same grammatical function, since the
     substitution of one for another does not disturb the syntax of a sentence.
    Linguistics often refers to the paradigmatic dimension of language as the ‗vertical axis‘ of selection
     (Oxford Concise Dictionary),
    Syntagmatic relations hold between two or more words co-present in a sequence. Combinations based on
     sequential relations are called syntagms.
    The notion of a syntagm applies among others to a group of words and to complex units of every size and
     kind, for example, phrases, sentences.
    Syntagm is a linguistic term designating any combination of units which are arranged in a significant
     sequence.
    A sentence is a syntagm of words.
    A meaning of a word is dependent partly on its relation to other words in the same conceptual area. The
     kinds of semantic fields vary from culture to culture.
    Anthropologists use them to study belief systems and reasoning across cultural groups.
    According to Brinton (2000), a semantic field denotes a segment of reality symbolized by a set of related
     words.
    The words in a semantic field share a common semantic property.
    Most often, fields are defined by subject matter, such as body parts, landforms, diseases, colors, foods, or
     kinship relations (Brinton, 2000).
    The words in a particular semantic field are ―incompatible‖ (Palmer, 1996).
    A creature cannot be denoted both as a lion and an elephant at the same time.
    Words in a semantic field are not synonymous, but are all used to talk about the same general phenomenon.
    The words anger, happiness, and sadness are not synonymous, but they are a part of the semantic field
     called ―emotional state‖.
    A collocation is either a highly frequent co-occurrence of two or more words or a combination of words
     which represents a fully grammatical structure, e.g. a noun phrase (Sinclair 2003: 173).
    Firth argued that "you shall know a word by the company it keeps" (1957: 11).
    Collocation is a familiar grouping of words, especially words that habitually appear together and thereby
     convey meaning by association.

    Collocations also define a sequence of words or terms that co-occur more often than would be expected by
     chance. e.g., Strong tea is a correct expression and Powerful tea is considered as the wrong expression.
    Idioms are expressions whose meaning cannot be inferred from the meaning of its parts.
    Usually, these are translated with semantically and not necessarily lexically equivalents in the target
     language.
    Majority of idioms are homophonous, such as ‗by and large‘ or ‗far and away‘ (Cruse, 1986: 37). They are
     grammatically well-formed and semantically transparent expressions.
    We cannot replace its parts with other semantically or syntactically equivalent lexemes.
    An idiom is a rigid word combination to which no generalities apply; neither can its meaning be determined
     from the meaning of its parts; nor can it participate in the usual word-order variations.
    Idioms involve collocation of a special kind, for instance, ‗kick the bucket‘, fly off the handle‘ and ‗red
     herring‘.

ENG508
➡️ Definition of Semantics and Pragmatics
Semantics studies the meaning of language, focusing on words, phrases, and sentences. Pragmatics
examines how context influences language interpretation.

➡️ The Borderline between Semantics and Pragmatics
The semantics-pragmatics boundary is blurry, as meaning depends on both linguistic structure and
contextual factors.

➡️ Sentence and Utterance
   -   Sentence: a linguistic unit
   -   Utterance: the spoken or written realization of a sentence

➡️ Language and Logic
Language and logic intersect in semantic analysis, using logical tools to understand linguistic
meaning.

➡️ The Explicit and the Implicit
   -   Explicit meaning: directly stated
   -   Implicit meaning: inferred from context

➡️ Semantics in Linguistics
Linguistic semantics investigates meaning within language systems.

➡️ Semantics in a Model of Grammar
Semantic components integrate with:
   -   Phonology
   -   Syntax
   -   Pragmatics

➡️ Historical Semantics
Historical semantics studies language meaning changes over time.

➡️ Semantics in Other Disciplines

Semantics intersects with:
   -   Philosophy
   -   Psychology
   -   Anthropology
   -   Computer Science

➡️ Semantics and Semiotics
   -   Semiotics: explores signs and symbols
   -   Semantics: focuses on linguistic meaning

➡️ Reference and Sense
   -   Reference: connects words to objects
   -   Sense: captures conceptual meaning

➡️ Utterance, Sentence, and Proposition
   -   Utterance: conveys a sentence
   -   Sentence: expresses a proposition (statement or assertion)

➡️ Literal and Non-Literal Meaning
   -   Literal meaning: direct
   -   Non-literal meaning: metaphor, irony, or inference

➡️ Theories of Meaning
Theories include:
   -   Idea Theory (mental concepts)
   -   Reference Theory (objective reference)
   -   Use Theory (language use)
   -   Truth-Conditional Theory (truth conditions)

➡️ What Is Meaning?
Meaning is the relationship between language and concept or object.

➡️ Meaning Holism
Meaning holism: meaning emerges from language as a whole.
Meaning within Language
Meaning determined by linguistic structure and context.

➡️ Idea Theory of Meaning
Idea Theory: meaning resides in mental concepts.

➡️ Meanings Are Out in the World
Reference Theory: meaning grounded in objective reality.
Some notable theories and models include:
   -   Truth-Conditional Semantics
   -   Model-Theoretic Semantics
   -   Relevance Theory
   -   Speech Act Theory
   -   Gricean Pragmatics

➡️ Meaning of Sentences and Truth Condition
Sentence meaning is determined by truth conditions, which specify when a sentence is true or
false.

➡️ Compositional Theory
Compositional theory posits that sentence meaning derives from combining word meanings.

➡️ Kinds of Meaning
   -   Linguistic/Conceptual Meaning: relates to word concepts
   -   Connotative/Referential Meaning: associates words with emotions or objects
   -   Social Meaning: reflects social context
   -   Affective Meaning: evokes emotions
   -   Reflective and Collocative Meaning: depends on word relationships
   -   Thematic Meaning: concerns sentence themes

➡️ Meaning, Thought, and Reality
   -   Sense and Concepts: words convey concepts
   -   Necessary and Sufficient Conditions: define concept boundaries
   -   Prototypes: concepts have central and peripheral instances
   -   Linguistic Relativity: language influences thought
   -   Language of Thought Hypothesis: thought precedes language

➡️ Lexical Relations
Lexical relations connect words:
   -   Synonyms (similar meaning)
   -   Antonyms (opposite meaning)
   -   Hyponym (specific to general)
   -   Meronym (part to whole)
   -   Homonym (same spelling, different meaning)
   -   Polysemy (related meanings)

➡️ Lexical Semantics: Fields and Collocation
   -   Semantic Fields: words group by meaning
   -   Collocations: word combinations
   -   Idioms: fixed expressions

➡️ Sentence Relations and Truth
   -   Logic and Truth: sentence truth conditions
   -   Propositional Logic: simple sentences
   -   Predicate Logic: complex sentences
   -   Entailment: logical implications
   -   Truth Conditional Semantics: sentence meaning from truth conditions

➡️ Presupposition
Presupposition assumes shared knowledge.

➡️ Tense and Aspect
Tense (time) and aspect (duration) modify verb meaning.

➡️ Modality
Modality expresses possibility, necessity, or obligation.

➡️ Mood
Mood conveys speaker attitude.

➡️ Evidentiality
Evidentiality indicates information sources.

➡️ Thematic Roles
Thematic roles identify participant relationships:
   -   Agent (actor)
   -   Patient (affected)
   -   Theme (object)
   -   Experiencer (feeling)
   -   Beneficiary (receiver)
   -   Instrument (means)
   -   Location (place)
   -   Goal (destination)
   -   Source (origin)
   -   Stimulus (trigger)

➡️ Grammatical Categories

Grammatical categories include:
   -   Nouns
   -   Verbs
   -   Adjectives
   -   Adverbs

➡️ Grammatical Relations
Grammatical relations connect words:
   -   Subject
   -   Object
   -   Modifier

➡️ Relationship with other Fields
Semantics intersects with philosophy, psychology, and computer sciEnce

➡️ Types of Lexical Rules
   -   Graded Accessibility
   -   Other Observations

➡️ What is Pragmatics?
Pragmatics studies how language users convey meaning in context, considering speaker intention,
listener interpretation, and social settings.

➡️ Types of Pragmatics
   -   Clinical Pragmatics (communication disorders)
   -   Developmental Pragmatics (language acquisition)
   -   Interlanguage Pragmatics (second language use)
   -   Neuropragmatics (brain-language relationships)
   -   Social Pragmatics (social interaction)

➡️ What Does Pragmatics Study?
Pragmatics examines:
   -   Speech acts (assertions, questions, commands)
   -   Implicature (implied meaning)
   -   Presupposition (assumed knowledge)
   -   Inference (derived meaning)
   -   Contextualization

Q. write a note on metaphor (3)(imp)
Metaphor is a type of figurative speech. Typically, a metaphor ascribes to an entity a property that
it does not, strictly and literally speaking, possess, although not all metaphors fit this definition.
Metaphors are not restricted to any particular type of word or phrase (Allott, 1988). The
metaphorical element of a sentence can be a noun phrase, as in ‗John is an iceberg.‘ Verbs can
also be used metaphorically, as in ‗Flintoff drilled the ball to the boundary.
Q. What Is the Perfect Aspect? (with Examples)
The perfect aspect (or complete aspect as it's sometimes called) is the aspect of a verb which
expresses a completed action. Perfect aspect is the term for verbs in a perfect tense. Examples of
Verbs in the Perfect Aspect We had seen. I had cleaned. She had drunk. How does traditional logic
concerns with semantics Traditional logic is also concerned with semantics as some of its
proposals range from simple syllogism to highly complex logical syntax. Logic makes use of
concepts found in ordinary language (‗and‘, ‗or‘, etc.).
Q. Social pragmatic
Social pragmatics which focuses on various aspects of the relationship between language use and
more general social and cultural factors. Social pragmatics is common with the fields such as
conversational analysis and discourse analysis.
Q. Tense and aspects
Tense is a category which allows a speaker to relate situations to time. EG they will cut the grass
tomorrow‘ is future tense. Aspect System allows the speaker to relate situation andtime, and to
view an event in various ways: as complete or incomplete. Aspects have to do not with the location
of an event in time, but with its temporal distribution or contour).
For example: She is coming.‘ (incomplete), ‗She has come.‘ (complete).

Define holism with example.

A word is defined in terms of some of the very words which help us to define. This
view is similar to ‗meaning holism‘ (Quine, 1960) – the meaning of a
word/phrase/ sentence depends on its relationship with other words, e.g. part of
what makes up the meaning of ‗tall‘ is that it is opposed to the meaning of ‗short‘.
Holist theory tends to be functional in the sense that it is some aspect of the uses of
a piece of language which makes for its meaning. If you call something ‗tall‘, you
should be willing to call it ‗not short‘.

Meaning holism may be correct in a way, it does not provide a basis for the
scientific study of linguistic meaning. That is why; it has not been appreciated by
formal semanticists (Portner, 2005, p. 3-5)
Define mood and its type subjunctive mood and imperative mood.

Mood is the quality of verb which conveys a writer‘s attitude or feelings towards a
subject (Saeed, 2004). Mood also shows the feelings of a speaker at time of

speaking. For example, ‗it may rain tomorrow. ‘In this example, the speaker‘s
attitude is uncertain about the rain. There are different types of moods:

Subjunctive moods contrast with indicative moods because there is an element of
uncertainty in subjunctive moods. These are used for wishes, beliefs, exhortations,
etc. e.g. ‗May you live long! (Saeed, 2004)

Imperative moods make direct commands or requests. For example, show me the
money.
What is Core vocabulary?

Each language has a core vocabulary of more frequent and basic words are widely
used in foreign language teaching. The core vocabulary could be used to trace
lexical links between languages to establish family relationships among them. The
implication of this approach is that the membership of core vocabulary will be the
same or similar for all languages. Swadesh originally proposed a 200-word list
which was later narrowed down to the 100-word list (see Saeed, 2014: 77).

Examples of Core Vocabulary Words

   •   Pronouns: I, you, it, they
   •   Verbs: go, do, make, have
   •   Adjectives: good, big, small, happy
   •   Prepositions: in, on, at, with

Repetition concern with linguistic.

The three concerns with repetition in linguistic studies discussed in the handouts
are:

Lexical Cohesion: Repetition is a tool for connecting ideas in a text. It helps
maintain coherence by repeating key words or phrases, which links parts of the text
together.

Avoidance of Redundancy: While repetition can help with clarity, it’s important
to avoid unnecessary repetition that could disrupt the flow of communication.
Using alternative linguistic devices like substitution or ellipsis can help avoid this.

Stylistic Effect: Repetition can also serve a stylistic function, adding emphasis or
rhythm to the speech or writing. However, too much repetition can make the text
monotonous, so it should be used carefully for impact without overdoing it.

Reasons behind introducing conceptual and procedural distinctions in
relevance.

The conceptual and procedural distinctions in relevance were introduced by Diane
Blakemore (1987) to account for differences in the meanings of regular content
words and discourse connectives. Conceptual meaning refers to the content or
concepts conveyed by words (like "dog" or "red"), whereas procedural meaning
refers to words that guide how the information should be processed (such as "but,"
"so," "therefore"). This distinction helps explain how words like "but" or "so"
influence the way listeners interpret the context of a conversation.

These distinctions are important because they clarify how language can
simultaneously carry information and guide the listener on how to use that
information within the conversation, reducing cognitive effort for comprehension .
What is Linguistic botanizing?

Austin organized a group of philosophers whose work is known as ordinary
language philosophy. The prevailing method was ‗linguistic botanizing‘; to see the
distinctions made by ordinary language on the assumption that the way people
speak makes many subtle distinctions, worthy of philosophical investigation. These
philosophers were drawn into thinking about questions such as ‗what saying or
stating involves‘and ‗what else speakers do with language‘.
Objections of Grice model.
Two main objections to Grice's Cooperative Principle are:

Assuming Everyone is Always Cooperative: Grice’s model assumes that people
always cooperate in conversations, but in real life, people sometimes want to speak
independently or avoid certain topics. This means not everyone follows the rules
all the time.

Cultural Differences: People from different cultures may understand and use
conversation rules in different ways. What might be acceptable in one culture (like
being vague or indirect) could be seen as violating the rules in another culture.

These objections highlight that Grice's model doesn't always fit how real
conversations happen across different cultures.
Explain violating the maxim relation and maxim manner.

Violating the maxim relation – Similarly, in answer to ‗How much did that new
dress cost?‘ the wife tries to distract him and change the topic saying: I know, let‘s
go out tonight. Now, where would you like to go? This shows the violation of the
maxim of relation.

Violating the maxim manner – In answer to ‗How much did that new dress cost?
‘, if she said that ‗a tiny fraction of my salary, though probably a bigger fraction of
the salary of the women that sold it to me‘, Hoping that it could be taken as an
answer and the matter could be dropped. It is, thus, like the wife answers the
question in a way that could be said to be violating the maxim of manner, in that
she says everything except what the husband wants to know.
Define transitive and intransitive?

Verbs that have objects are called transitive verbs and those without objects are

Q What is Semantics?

      ENG508 Midterm Short Notes BY PIN2 and MUHAMMAD (MAS All Rounder)

      ENG508 Midterm Short Notes BY PIN2 and MUHAMMAD (MAS All Rounder)

        The field of linguistics which is concerned with the study of meaning in language is called
Semantics. Semantics is the part of linguistics that is concerned with the study of literal, de-
contextualized and grammatical meaning (Frawley, 1992). Semantics can also refer to the branch of
study within linguistics that deals with language and how we understand meaning. This has been a
particularly interesting field for philosophers as they debate the essence of meaning, how we build
meaning, how we share meaning with others, and how meaning changes over time. Linguistic
semantics is the study of how languages organize and express meanings (Kreidler, 1998)..

Q What is Pragmatics?
 Pragmatics is a branch of linguistics, which is the study of language. Pragmatics focuses on
conversational implicature, which is a process in which the speaker implies and a listener infers. Simply
put, pragmatics studies language that is not directly spoken. Instead, the speaker hints at or suggests a
meaning, and the listener assumes the correct intention.

         Pragmatics is the study of meaning as communicated by the speaker and interpreted by the
listener”. According to Yule (2010), ‘Pragmatics is the study of “invisible” meaning, or how we recognize
what is meant even when it isn’t actually said or written’. This includes background knowledge context
i.e. people know about each other and the world. Pragmatics may vary from culture to culture.

Q Differentiate Utterances, Sentences, and Proposition.
     Utterance
 Definition:An utterance is any stretch of talk, by one person, before and after which there is silence on
the part of that person.

Rule: An utterance is the use by a particular speaker, on a particular occasion, of a piece of language,
such as a sequence of sentences, or a single phrase, or even a single word.
Example:‘Hello’, ‘Not much’ are utterances.Where as,‘Pxgotmgt’ and

‘Schplotzenpflaaaaaaargh!’ are not utterances because these strings of sounds is not from any
language.

      Sentence
Definition: A sentence is neither a physical event nor a physical object. It is, conceived abstractly, a
string of words put together by the grammatical rules of a language. A sentence can be thought of as the
ideal string of words behind various realizations in utterances and inscriptions.

Rule: We have defined a sentence as a string of words. A given sentence always consists of the same
words, and in the same order. Any change in the words, or in their order, makes a different sentence,
for our purposes.

Example:
       a) Helen rolled up the carpet

        a)Sincerity may frighten the boy

      ENG508 Midterm Short Notes BY PIN2 and MUHAMMAD (MAS All Rounder)

     Proposition
Definition: A proposition is that part of the meaning of the utterance of a declarative sentence which
describes some state of affairs.

        The field of linguistics which is concerned with the study of meaning in language is called
Semantics. Semantics is the part of linguistics that is concerned with the study of literal, de-
contextualized and grammatical meaning (Frawley, 1992). Semantics can also refer to the branch of
study within linguistics that deals with language and how we understand meaning. This has been a
particularly interesting field for philosophers as they debate the essence of meaning, how we build
meaning, how we share meaning with others, and how meaning changes over time. Linguistic
semantics is the study of how languages organize and express meanings (Kreidler, 1998)..

Q What is Pragmatics?
 Pragmatics is a branch of linguistics, which is the study of language. Pragmatics focuses on
conversational implicature, which is a process in which the speaker implies and a listener infers. Simply
put, pragmatics studies language that is not directly spoken. Instead, the speaker hints at or suggests a
meaning, and the listener assumes the correct intention.

         Pragmatics is the study of meaning as communicated by the speaker and interpreted by the
listener”. According to Yule (2010), ‘Pragmatics is the study of “invisible” meaning, or how we recognize
what is meant even when it isn’t actually said or written’. This includes background knowledge context
i.e. people know about each other and the world. Pragmatics may vary from culture to culture.

string of words put together by the grammatical rules of a language. A sentence can be thought of as the
ideal string of words behind various realizations in utterances and inscriptions.

words, and in the same order. Any change in the words, or in their order, makes a different sentence,

Implicit:
Implicit meaning refers to the underlying or implied significance of a word, phrase,
or expression that may not be explicitly stated. It involves the unspoken connotations,
suggestions, or interpretations that are conveyed indirectly and are often dependent
on context, cultural understanding, or shared knowledge.
For example, the tone of voice, body language, or cultural references in a
conversation can convey implicit meanings that add depth and layers of interpretation
beyond the explicit words spoken.

4. What is meant by the term “logic” in language?
Ans: Logic is concerned with ways in which ideas relate to each other, can be
combined together and can be used to derive other ideas with confidence. Logicians
tend not to talk about ‗ideas‘ though; the basic unit of traditional logic is the
‗proposition‘; a significant term in the discussions of meanings in linguistics.

                                      CHAPTER 2

1. Describe semantics according to Palmer and saeed?
Ans: Semantics is a technical term used to refer to the study of meanings. The
meaning covers a variety of aspects of the language but unfortunately, there is no
general consideration to describe it (Palmer, 1997).
Modern linguistics includes various meditations regarding the knowledge of
linguistics, i.e. how to pronounce the words, construct sentences and meanings (Saeed,
2004)
2. How Chomsky define semantic ?
Ans: Chomsky, in particular, has commented on the creativity of the sentence
formation. It is one of the generative grammar‘s most important insights that
relatively a small number of combination rules allow the speakers to use a finite set of
words to create a very large and infinite number of sentences.
3. Define semiotic ?
Ans: Semiotics is the study of signs and symbols and their interpretation, particularly
how meaning is conveyed through various elements such as language, images, sounds,
and gestures. It is a field that examines the processes of signification and
communication in different forms, exploring how signs and symbols function in
conveying meaning within a specific cultural or social context.
In semiotics, a "sign" is a basic unit of meaning, and it can take various forms. There
are typically three components to a sign:

1. Signifier: This is the physical form of the sign, such as a word, image, sound, or
gesture.

2. Signified:This is the concept or idea represented by the signifier. It is the meaning
associated with the sign.

3. Referent: In some cases, there might be a real-world object or phenomenon to
which the sign refers. This is known as the referent.

Semiotics encompasses both verbal and non-verbal communication, and it is used to
analyze how signs and symbols operate in different cultural, social, and linguistic
contexts.

Definition of Semantics and Pragmatics
   - Semantics: the study of meaning in language, focusing on the meaning
      of words, phrases, sentences, and texts.
   - Pragmatics: the study of how language is used in context to
      communicate effectively, considering factors like speaker intention,
      audience, and social norms.
The Borderline between Semantics and Pragmatics: The distinction
between semantics and pragmatics can be blurry, as meaning is often
dependent on context.
Sentence and Utterance
   - Sentence: a unit of language that expresses a complete thought or idea.
   - Utterance: a specific instance of a sentence being used in a particular
      context.
Language and Logic: Language and logic are closely related, as language is
used to express logical ideas and relationships.
The Explicit and the Implicit
   - Explicit meaning: the literal or obvious meaning of a sentence or text.
   - Implicit meaning: the implied or suggested meaning that goes beyond
      the literal interpretation.
Semantics in Linguistics: Semantics is a key area of study in linguistics,
exploring how meaning is created and conveyed through language.
Semantics in a Model of Grammar: A model of grammar that includes
semantics aims to explain how meaning is generated from the structure of
language.
Historical Semantics: Historical semantics examines how word meanings
change over time.

Semantics in Other Disciplines: Semantics is also relevant in fields like
philosophy, computer science, and anthropology.
Semantics and Semiotics: Semiotics is the study of signs and symbols, and
semantics is a key part of this field.
Reference and Sense
   - Reference: the relationship between a word or phrase and the thing it
       refers to.
   - Sense: the meaning of a word or phrase in a particular context.
Utterance, Sentence and Proposition
   - Utterance: a specific instance of a sentence being used.
   - Sentence: a unit of language that expresses a complete thought.
   - Proposition: the meaning or idea expressed by a sentence.
Utterance, Sentence and Proposition -Activities: These terms are related to
how language is used to communicate and convey meaning.
Literal and Non-Literal Meaning
   - Literal meaning: the obvious or explicit meaning of a sentence or text.
   - Non-literal meaning: the implied or suggested meaning that goes
       beyond the literal interpretation.
Semantics and Pragmatics: Semantics focuses on the meaning of language,
while pragmatics considers how language is used to communicate effectively.
Meaning Holism -Meaning within Language: Meaning holism suggests
that meaning is not just a matter of individual words or phrases, but of the
entire language system.
Idea Theory of Meaning: This theory posits that meaning is based on the
ideas or concepts that words and phrases represent.
Meanings Are out in the World: This perspective suggests that meaning is
not just a matter of language, but of the world and our experiences in it.
Meaning of Sentences and Truth Condition: The meaning of a sentence is
closely tied to its truth condition, or the circumstances under which it is true.
Putting Meaning Together from Pieces – Compositional Theory: This
theory suggests that meaning is composed of smaller parts, such as words and
phrases, that combine to create the meaning of a sentence or text.
KINDS OF MEANING

     - Linguistic/Conceptual Meaning: the meaning of words and phrases
        based on their linguistic structure and conceptual relationships.
     - Connotative/Referential Meaning: the emotional or associative
        meaning of words (connotative) versus their literal reference
        (referential).
     - Social Meaning: the meaning derived from social context, norms, and
        relationships.
     - Affective Meaning: the emotional or attitudinal meaning of words and
        phrases.
     - Reflective and Collocative Meaning: the meaning derived from the
        relationship between words and their contexts (collocative) and the
        reflection of meaning back on the speaker (reflective).
     - Thematic Meaning: the underlying theme or idea conveyed by a text
        or discourse.
   MEANING, THOUGHT AND REALITY
     - Sense and Concepts: the meaning of words and phrases is related to
        the concepts they represent.
     - Necessary and Sufficient Conditions: the conditions under which a
        word or phrase applies to a concept or object.
     - Prototypes: the central, typical instances of a concept or category.
     - Linguistic Relativity: the idea that language influences thought and
        perception.
     - The Language of Thought Hypothesis: the idea that thought is
        conducted in a mental language.
   What are Lexical Relations?
Lexical relations refer to the relationships between words and their meanings,
including:
      -   Synonyms (words with similar meanings)
      -   Antonyms (words with opposite meanings)
      -   Hyponyms (words with more specific meanings)
      -   Meronyms (words with part-whole relationships)
      -   Causative verbs and agentive nouns (words that express cause-and-
          effect relationships)

      - Colour terms (words that describe colours)
   Words and Lexical Items: Words are the basic units of language, while
   lexical items are the specific instances of words in context.
   Problems with Pinning Down Word Meaning
Word meaning can be difficult to define due to:
      - Homonymy (words with multiple meanings)
      - Polysemy (words with related meanings)
      - Contextual variation
      - Semantic change over time
   LEXICAL SEMANTICS: FIELDS AND COLLOCATION
      - Pragmatic and Syntagmatic Relations: the relationships between
         words based on their use in context (pragmatic) and their grammatical
         relationships (syntagmatic).
      - Semantic Fields: the areas of meaning that words and concepts occupy,
         such as "food" or "emotions".
      - Collocations: the common combinations of words that occur together,
         such as "strong coffee" or "happy birthday".

INTRODUCTION TO SEMANTICS AND PRAGMATICS

Topic-001: Definition of Semantics and Pragmatics Learning Theories

What is semantics?

Semantics is the study of literal, de-contextualized, and grammatical meaning in
language.

How is linguistic semantics defined?

Linguistic semantics is the study of how languages organize and express
meanings.

What does semantics analyze in language?

Semantics analyzes the relationships between signs, symbols, and their
representations.

Define pragmatics.

 COMPILED BY SIR ZAHID                                                             1

Pragmatics is the study of meaning as communicated by the speaker and
interpreted by the listener.

How does Yule describe pragmatics?

Pragmatics is the study of "invisible" meaning, recognizing implied meaning
beyond the literal words.

What does pragmatics consider in communication?

Pragmatics considers context, background knowledge, and cultural variations in
communication.

What is semantics and what does it study?

Semantics refers to the branch of linguistics that concerns itself with the study of
literal, de-contextualized, and grammatical meaning. It analyzes how languages
organize and express meanings. Linguistic semantics explores the relationships
between linguistic signs, symbols, and their representations.

Define pragmatics and its scope.

Pragmatics is the study of meaning as communicated by a speaker and
interpreted by a listener. It delves into the "invisible" meaning that goes beyond
the explicit words used. This field includes context, background knowledge, and
cross-cultural variations in communication

Topic-002: The Borderline between Semantics and Pragmatics

What does semantics study?

Semantics studies the contribution of linguistic items' meanings and their
combinations to overall meaning.

Describe lexical semantics.

Lexical semantics deals with the meanings of individual words.

What is compositional semantics concerned with?

 COMPILED BY SIR ZAHID                                                               2

Compositional semantics studies how word meanings combine to form phrase
and sentence meanings.

Where does pragmatics focus in relation to semantics?

Pragmatics focuses on the meaning conveyed by an utterance in a specific context
after semantics.

Explain the difference between semantics and pragmatics.

Semantics is concerned with the meanings contributed by linguistic items and
how they combine to form meaning. On the other hand, pragmatics deals with
the meaning conveyed by an utterance in a specific context. Pragmatics takes
over where semantics ends, focusing on context-specific interpretations.

Topic-003: Sentences and Utterances

What does semantics deal with in terms of linguistic entities?

Semantics deals with the meaning of sentences.

What is the distinction between sentences and utterances?

other words, it allows us to understand and conceptualize the meaning of words
by associating them with mental images or representations. This connection
between words and mental representations is fundamental in understanding how
we convey and comprehend meaning through language.

Topic 29: Necessary and Sufficient Conditions

What is the traditional approach for describing concepts?

Necessary and sufficient conditions are used to describe concepts.

What are necessary conditions in the context of concepts?

Necessary conditions are attributes that something must have to be considered
an example of a concept.

What are sufficient conditions in the context of concepts?

Sufficient conditions are the right set of conditions that define a concept fully.

Topic 30: Prototypes

How is the model of concepts as prototypes structured?

Concepts are structured with central, typical members and less typical or
peripheral members.

How do experiments support prototype theory?

 COMPILED BY SIR ZAHID                                                               2

Speakers tend to agree more readily on typical members, which come to mind
more quickly.

The prototypical conception emphasizes typical members and the gradient nature

The model of concepts as prototypes is structured in a way that acknowledges the
existence of central or typical members within a category, such as "BIRD" or
"FURNITURE." In this model, there are central members that are considered
highly typical and representative of a particular category. These central members
gradually transition into less typical or peripheral members, which do not exhibit
all the typical characteristics but still belong to the same category.

It suggests that the language we speak conditions our conceptualization and is
influenced by culture.

Cognitive science rejects linguistic relativity and argues that thinking can occur

The model of concepts as prototypes is structured in a way that acknowledges the
existence of central or typical members within a category, such as "BIRD" or
"FURNITURE." In this model, there are central members that are considered
highly typical and representative of a particular category. These central members
gradually transition into less typical or peripheral members, which do not exhibit
all the typical characteristics but still belong to the same category.

Topic 31: Linguistic Relativity

Who are the key figures associated with the notion of linguistic relativity?

Edward Sapir and Benjamin Lee Whorf are associated with linguistic relativity.

What does linguistic relativity propose regarding language and thought?

It suggests that the language we speak conditions our conceptualization and is
influenced by culture.

Topic 32: The Language of Thought Hypothesis

Why do proponents of cognitive science reject linguistic relativity?

Cognitive science rejects linguistic relativity and argues that thinking can occur
without language.

What is the "language of thought hypothesis"?

It posits that cognitive processes use a separate computational system in the
mind, a "language of thought."

How do proponents of the "language of thought" view the relationship between
thought and spoken language?

They believe that we think in a language of thought (Mentalese) and translate it
into spoken language when needed.

Topic 33: What Are Lexical Relations?

What is the branch of semantics that deals with word meanings called?

Lexical semantics.

How would you define lexical relations?

Lexical relations are relationships of the meanings of words to other words.

What types of relations do lexical relations encompass, aside from semantic
relations?

Lexical relations include phonetic relations such as rhyme and alliteration,
morphological relations such as inflectional variations, and morpho-syntactic
relations such as co-membership in a grammatical category.

What does the term "lexical relation" encompass, and how does it differ from
just a semantic relation?

The term "lexical relation" includes phonetic relations like rhyme and alliteration,
morphological relations such as inflectional variations, and morpho-syntactic
relations like co-membership in a grammatical category. It goes beyond just
semantic relations and contributes to the network-like structure of our mental
lexicon.

Topic 34: Words and Lexical Items

What is the focus of interest in semantic relations?

Lexemes or semantic words.

How do words differ in their representation in different linguistic levels (writing,
phonology, syntax)?

Words can be identified in writing by white spaces, in phonology as strings of
sounds, and in syntax, they can have various grammatical variations.

What is a lexeme in semantics?

A lexeme is the same semantic word represented by several grammatically
distinct variations.

The influence of context on word meanings.

Lesson 11

                          PRESUPPOSITION
Topic 54: Introduction to Presupposition

What does presupposition mean in ordinary language?

Presupposition in ordinary language means to assume something.

How is presupposition defined in semantics?

Presupposition in semantics refers to assumptions implicitly made by speakers
and listeners necessary for correct interpretation.

Topic 55: Two Approaches to Presupposition

How are sentences viewed in the first approach to presupposition?

COMPILED BY SIR ZAHID                                                           1

In the first approach, sentences are viewed as external objects, and the process of
producing them is not a concern.

What is the focus of the second approach to presupposition?

The second approach views sentences as the utterances of individuals engaged in
a communication act, focusing on the strategies used in communication.

Topic 56: Presupposition Failure

What is presupposition failure?

Presupposition failure occurs when using a name or definite description
presupposes the existence of the named or described entity.

In the case of presupposition failure, what happens when there is no referent
for the nominal?

If there is no referent for the nominal, the sentences may be in a grey area,
possibly neither true nor false.

Topic 57: Presupposition Triggers

What are presupposition triggers?

Presupposition triggers are types of presupposition produced by specific words or
constructions, often derived from syntactic structures.

Give an example of a lexical trigger for presupposition.

Verbs like 'regret' and 'realize' are lexical triggers because they presuppose the
truth of their complement clause.

Topic 58: Presupposition and Context

Why is there a problem for a simple truth-based account of presupposition?

Presuppositional behavior appears sensitive to context, creating challenges for a
simple truth-based account.

 COMPILED BY SIR ZAHID                                                               2

What is defeasibility in the context of presupposition?

Defeasibility is the characteristic of presupposition where it can be canceled by
general knowledge or context, as seen in example 2 with the verb "died."

  Lesson 12
          SENTENCE SEMANTICS - I: SITUATIONS
Topic 59: Introduction to Classifying Situations

How does language allow the classification of situations?

Language classifies situations through semantic distinctions of actions, states,
processes, tenses, and aspects.

What are two common types of situations based on lexical categories in verbs?

Two common types are stative (e.g., knows, thinks) and dynamic (e.g., eat, drive)
situations.

Topic 60: Tense and Aspect

What does tense allow a speaker to relate situations to?

Tense allows a speaker to relate situations to time.

How does the aspect system relate to events?

The aspect system allows the speaker to view an event in various ways, such as
complete or incomplete.

Topic 61: Modality

What is modality, and how does it modify the meaning of an event?

 COMPILED BY SIR ZAHID                                                              3

Modality is a linguistic category that modifies the meaning of an event, expressing
ways to "influence" the event, including giving permission, describing ability,
suggesting, etc.

What are the two types of modality?

Epistemic Modality (degree of knowledge) and Deontic Modality (attitude to
social factors of obligation, responsibility, and permission).

Topic 62: Mood

What is mood in the context of verbs?

Mood is the quality of a verb that conveys a writer’s attitude or feelings towards a
subject.

Provide examples of different types of moods.

Indicative moods: express facts, opinions, or questions based on realist form.

Potential moods: indicate probability.

Subjunctive moods: used for wishes, beliefs, exhortations, etc.

Imperative moods: make direct commands or requests.

Topic 63: Evidentiality

What is evidentiality, and what does it communicate?

Evidentiality is a semantic category allowing a speaker to communicate their
attitude to the source of information, indicating whether it relies on personal
first-hand knowledge or another source.

Name different types of evidentiality.

Witness Evidentiality: information from direct observation.

Sensory Evidentiality: speaker’s evidence from sensory experience.

 COMPILED BY SIR ZAHID                                                            4

Inferential Evidentiality: statement based on deduction from facts.

Reportative Evidentiality: information reported by another person.

Assumed Evidentiality: information based on general knowledge or habitual
activities.

Topic 64: Introduction: Classifying Participants

What are some semantic labels for roles in linguistics?

Participant roles (Allan, 1986)

Deep semantic cases (Fillmore, 1968)

Semantic roles (Givon, 1990)

Thematic roles (Dowty, 1991; Jackendoff, 1990)

What is the distinction between grammatical relations and semantic roles?

Grammatical relations are morphosyntactic.

Semantic roles (e.g., agent, patient) are conceptual notions.

Topic 65: Thematic Roles – I (Agent, Patient, Theme, Experiencer)

Define 'Agent' in thematic roles.

The initiator of an action with volition.

Provide an example of 'Patient' in thematic roles.

John cut down these bushes.

Entity changed or moved by a verb's action.

Define 'Experiencer' in thematic roles.

Entity aware of the action or state but not in control.

Politeness Theory

Developed by Brown and Levinson, this theory suggests people maintain “face” (public self-
image) in interaction. Politeness strategies are used to avoid threatening another's face.

Concept of Face in Politeness

“Face” refers to an individual’s self-image in a social context. Two types:

      Positive face: desire to be liked, appreciated.
      Negative face: desire for autonomy and freedom from imposition.

Positive and Negative Face

      Positive face: Need to be accepted by others (e.g., compliments).
      Negative face: Need not to be imposed upon (e.g., apologies, indirect requests).

Face Threatening Act (FTA) & Face Saving Act (FSA)

      FTA: Any act that threatens the hearer’s or speaker’s face (e.g., “Shut the window!”).
      FSA: Strategies to minimize threat (e.g., “Could you please close the window?”).

Three Maxims of Politeness

   1. Tact Maxim – minimize cost to others.
   2. Generosity Maxim – minimize benefit to self.
   3. Approbation Maxim – avoid dispraise of others.

What Happens When a Polite Form Is Used Inappropriately?

It may cause confusion, awkwardness, or unintended offense. For example, over-politeness in
informal situations can seem sarcastic or distant.

Topic – 119 Properties of Conversational Implicature

Cancellability is one of the properties of conversational implicature. It is also known as defeasibility. Presence of a
conversational implicature relies on a number of factors such as the conventional meaning of words used, the
linguistic and situational contexts, etc. So if any of them changes, the implicature will also change.

Non-detachability - a conversational implicature is attached to the semantic content of what is said, not to the
linguistic form i.e. it is possible to use a synonym and keep the implicature intact. It will not be detached from the
utterance as a whole, even though the specific words may be changed.

Reinforceability - Implicatures can be reinforced, e.g. John answered most of the questions. But he wasn‘t able to
answer the last question. (not redundant)

Non-conventionality - implicature is not carried by what is said, but only by the saying of what is said, or by
‗putting it that way.‘

 Calculability – speakers try to convey conversational implicatures and hearers are able to understand them suggests
that implicatures are calculable.

Topic – 120 Conventional Implicature

Conventional implicature is not based on the cooperative principle or the maxims. They do not have to occur in a
conversation. They do not depend on special contexts for their interpretation. However, they are associated with
specific words that result in additional conveyed meanings when used. The English conjunction ‗but‘ is one of these
words.

The interpretation of any utterance of the type ‗p but q‘ will be based on the conjunction ‗p & q‘ plus an implicature
of ‗contrast‘ between the information in ‗p‘ and the information in ‗q‘. Other English words such as ‗even‘ and
‗yet‘ also have conventional implicatures.

Topic – 121 Properties of Conventional Implicature

Non-truth-conditionality - conventional implicature do not make any contribution to truth conditions e.g. a) we want
peace and they want war. b) we want peace but they want war. Both ‗a‘ and ‗b‘ shares the same truth conditions.
